item.title: Stochastic climate emulation at reduced cost with ACE2.5-ERA5
item.description: arXiv:2611.28315v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce ACE2.5-ERA5 (Ai2 Climate Emulator of ERA5, version 2.5), a stochastic autoregressive weather-climate AI model that produces calibrated weather ensembles with realistic small-scale structure on timescales from days to centuries. Its deterministic predecessor, ACE2-ERA5, retains 36% of its ERA5 target's precipitation spectral power at total wavenumbers 100--179; ACE2.5-ERA5 retains 86%. In weather forecasts its ensemble spread matches its error to within 4% from day 3. Time-mean climate is on par with or better than ACE2-ERA5, the precipitation response to ENSO is improved, and the model is stable over 1000 years. Interannual variability of global mean surface temperature is shown not to be calibrated in either ACE2.5-ERA5 or its predecessor. ACE2.5-ERA5 differs from ACE2-ERA5 in three ways. Noise-conditioned layer normalization, trained with a combined CRPS and spectral energy score loss in place of mean squared error, makes it stochastic. Spectral bottlenecking with grouped convolutions cuts the Spherical Fourier Neural Operator's spectral filter parameters by more than two orders of magnitude and leaves a model a tenth the size of ACE2-ERA5. Its time step is daily rather than 6-hourly. ACE2.5-ERA5 has 3.2 times the inference throughput of ACE2-ERA5. A 6-hourly variant has weather prediction skill similar to ACE2-ERA5. A 4-degree variant reaches comparable climate skill at an order of magnitude lower training cost, enabling rapid iteration during development. We release 1-degree daily, 4-degree daily and 1-degree 6-hourly checkpoints.
item.dc:creator: Jeremy McGibbon, Troy Arcomano, Spencer K. Clark, James P. C. Duncan, Brian Henn, Oliver Watt-Meyer

item.title: Competing climates of the present-day Earth: from Snowball to Hothouse
item.description: arXiv:2611.28357v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Earth today has one climate, but it could have others. With the same continents, the same solar constant and the same pre-industrial CO2, our planet could settle into strikingly different ones. We explore this possibility with BIG-MITgcm, a model which couples atmosphere and ocean circulation with ice sheets and vegetation, and which can be integrated over many millennia. We find five different climates and describe them here. At one extreme is a Snowball, with ice from pole to pole. A Waterbelt also exists, in which sea ice reaches the tropics and only a thin equatorial ribbon of open ocean survives. There is a Cold world much like the Last Glacial Maximum, a Warm climate in which we live in today, and a Hot world in which the Atlantic overturning circulation has collapsed. Each state is held in place by its own balance of competing feedbacks. Ocean heat transport anchors each climate, holding the ice edge where that transport is weak. The familiar climate of the past 10 thousand years is perhaps just one of several possibilities. This has implications for glacial-interglacial transitions and the risk of crossing global tipping points in the future.
item.dc:creator: Laure Moinat, John Marshall, Maura Brunetti

item.title: Diurnal Warm Layer and Marginal Instability in the Ocean Surface Boundary Layer
item.description: arXiv:2611.28422v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large-eddy simulations with high near-surface grid resolution are used to investigate the diurnal modulation of the ocean surface boundary layer (OSBL) at various latitudes for Coriolis frequencies corresponding to 15-70$^\circ$N. The OSBL, which is driven here by a low wind, surface waves and a diurnally varying heat flux, exhibits a diurnal warm layer (DWL) during daytime and a convective mixing layer at night. The DWL exhibits enhanced shear leading to daytime turbulence that is found in this study to exist in a state of marginal instability (MI) over a wide range of latitudes and convective heat fluxes. The MI is characterized by an intricate balance between the momentum input by wind, stable stratification owing to solar radiation and turbulent mixing in the DWL, such that the gradient Richardson number is maintained around the critical value of 0.25 from morning to late afternoon. The enhanced shear and stratification sustained by MI leads to a substantial deviation from Monin-Obukhov Similarity Theory. Turbulent mixing induced by MI is shown to be similar to isolated local Kelvin-Helmholtz shear instability events and to share a similar range of flux coefficients and flux Richardson numbers. The impacts of increasing rotation and nightly convection on OSBL variability at the inertial and diurnal timescales are quantified through a turbulent kinetic energy analysis. The interaction between inertial oscillations and diurnal shear is an important feature of the DWL at mid and high latitudes.
item.dc:creator: Adam Joseph Hall, Hieu Tan Pham, Sophia Merrifield, Sutanu Sarkar

item.title: Classifying detectability and time of emergence across different Stratospheric Aerosol Injection strategies
item.description: arXiv:2611.28455v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Stratospheric aerosol injection (SAI) can be deployed using different injection strategies with the same global-mean cooling target and result in distinct regional climate responses. The ability to identify the deployed strategy from observed climate depends on how large the regional differences are relative to internal variability. In this study, we ask whether five feedback-controlled SAI strategies from the GAUSS ensemble (CESM2(WACCM6), SSP2-4.5), all targeting 1.0$^\circ$C above pre-industrial levels, can be distinguished from annual global and regional means of near-surface temperature, precipitation, and polar sea-ice fraction, and when this distinguishability emerges. We use multinomial logistic-regression classifiers with leave-one-member-out cross-validation and define the emergence year using a family-wise error rate threshold computed from a restricted-permutation null, combined with a calibrated persistence requirement. We find that the strategies become distinguishable in the mid-to-late 2040s, about 8-14 years after deployment, with a peak accuracy of 0.87 on a model using both global and regional features. Additionally, we find that no model trained on a single region-variable pair performs as well as the models using global and regional means, suggesting the discriminative signal is small and distributed across regions and variables. The equatorial and high-latitude injection strategies are the most distinguishable. The classifier is able to recognize the multi-latitude strategy more easily at lower temperature targets. Our results suggest that annual climate features can identify with confidence which coordinated injection strategy has been deployed roughly a decade or more after deployment.
item.dc:creator: Sai Charan Petchetti, Daniele Visioni

item.title: LayerCake v1.0: a framework for low- to intermediate-order automated models development
item.description: arXiv:2611.28647v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A new model development framework called LayerCake is presented. It is written in the Python language and relies on the Sympy symbolic computation package to compute the Galerkin projection of two-dimensional spatially extended geophysical models. These projections provide their time evolution operator in the spectral space on a restricted set of modes. The resulting tendencies of the models can be evaluated either numerically (for time integration) or symbolically (for parameters sensitivity analysis and bifurcation analysis). We provide several simple examples of geophysical models to showcase the capabilities of the framework, and we hint at how more complex systems can be designed.
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Demaeyer, Ois\'in Hamilton, St\'ephane Vannitsem

item.title: Lagrangian particle simulations of an idealized deep convective squall line: Aggregation, fragmentation, and their polarimetric signatures
item.description: arXiv:2611.28805v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate secondary ice production (SIP) in an idealized deep convective squall line using the Lagrangian particle model McSnow coupled to ICON. The model represents ice particle properties, including habit, riming degree, and mass composition. We introduce a parameterization of collision-induced ice--ice fragmentation linked to apparent density as a measure of particle fragility. We compare rime splintering (RS), freezing fragmentation (FF), and collision-induced fragmentation (CF), including turbulence-enhanced collision rates. Collision-induced fragmentation is the dominant SIP mechanism, strongly increasing ice number concentrations in the dendritic growth zone. Freezing fragmentation contributes little because sufficiently large raindrops are scarce. Rime splintering produces secondary ice at lower altitudes and indirectly promotes large aggregates. Turbulence has little effect on fragmentation but enhances the aggregation of fragments. Fragmentation shifts the particle size distribution toward smaller sizes and reduces precipitation, while turbulence-enhanced aggregation partly restores large particles and precipitation. McRadar forward simulations show that SIP affects radar moments and Doppler spectra. Specific differential phase KDP provides the clearest conventional radar signature of fragmentation. Spectral differential reflectivity identifies secondary ice source regions through enhanced signals at the slow edge of the Doppler spectrum. Our results identify collision-induced fragmentation as a key source of secondary ice in deep convection and show that its impact depends on interactions with aggregation and turbulence. Spectral polarimetric radar observations may help constrain SIP in nature.
item.dc:creator: Axel Seifert, Fabian Jakub, Christoph Siewert, Mikl\'os Szak\'all, Leonie von Terzi, Stefan Kneifel

item.title: Tipping cascades may lock the Earth system on a pathway towards a melthouse
item.description: arXiv:2611.29086v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The potential for the Earth system to transition irreversibly into a hothouse Earth has attracted considerable scientific and media attention but remains insufficiently explored in modeling studies. Using a reduced-complexity Earth system model that includes a dynamic carbon cycle and interacting tipping elements, we find no planetary threshold beyond which the Earth system irreversibly shifts into a hothouse state. Instead, tipping cascades can drive the system towards an irreversible melthouse state with over 10 m of sea-level rise. Such cascades may occur even under low-emission scenarios, preventing long-term stabilization of sea level at intermediate values. Our results overall highlight the substantial risk of a melthouse rather than a hothouse Earth, and call for drastic emission reductions to avert dramatic impacts on coastal cities and communities.
item.dc:creator: Victor Couplet, Wim Thiery, Michel Crucifix

item.title: China daily CO2 emission estimates 2019-2025
item.description: arXiv:2611.29938v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Near-real-time CO2 estimates enable timely tracking of emission changes, but broad sectoral classifications limit their ability to resolve industrial dynamics across China's provinces. Here, we update Carbon Monitor to estimate daily CO2 emissions across five sectors in 31 mainland Chinese provinces during 2019-2025 and monthly emissions from 40 industrial and construction subsectors in 30 provinces, combining historical inventories with industrial production indicators. National emissions increased from 10.83 Gt CO2 in 2019 to 12.15 Gt CO2 in 2023, before declining slightly to 12.08 Gt CO2 in 2025. The 2024-2025 national reduction of 0.23% reflected opposing sectoral trends, with industrial emissions increasing by 48.8 Mt CO2 while power generation and ground transport emissions decreased by 46.6 Mt CO2 and 27.7 Mt CO2, respectively. Provincial trajectories also diverged, with emissions rising in 16 provinces and falling in 15. Industrial disaggregation revealed increases of 102.3 Mt CO2 in nonferrous-metal smelting and pressing and decreases of 108.1 Mt CO2 in nonmetal mineral products during 2019-2024. Comparison with a historical provincial inventory yielded a median absolute relative difference of 9.4%. These findings demonstrate that national emission stabilization masks divergent regional and industrial changes, highlighting the need for temporally updated, sector-specific evidence to assess progress toward sustained reductions and identify mitigation priorities.
item.dc:creator: Xiaoting Huang, Zhu Deng, Ling Ye, Peng Lu, Xuanren Song, Yuli Shan, Zhu Liu

item.title: Global Patterns and Drivers of Terrestrial Surface Albedo Dynamics from 2001 to 2025
item.description: arXiv:2611.29961v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Terrestrial surface albedo is a fundamental determinant of the global radiative balance, yet a spatially integrated understanding of its long-term trajectories and multi-sphere environmental drivers remains lacking. Utilizing MODIS observations (2001-2025), this study integrates Theil-Sen trend analysis, standardized anomaly diagnostics, and a pixel-wise multiple linear regression framework to quantify global albedo dynamics and attribute them to biophysical drivers. Our results reveal that global albedo change is characterized by profound spatial heterogeneity rather than a uniform trend, with 23.3% of the land surface exhibiting significant brightening, while 18.9% showed significant darkening. Multi-driver attribution demonstrates a clear zonal organization of controls: snow cover dominates albedo variability in northern high latitudes (46.9% of classified area), while NDVI (41.0%) and soil moisture (12.1%) govern tropical vegetated regions and moisture-limited transitional zones, respectively. These findings underscore that while terrestrial albedo is a robust indicator of Earth system change, its interpretation depends strongly on regional cryospheric, biophysical, and hydrological contexts.
item.dc:creator: Xiaoting Huang, Zhu Liu

item.title: COSIMA Cookbook: a community-driven resource for ocean and sea-ice modelling science
item.description: arXiv:2611.30182v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The COSIMA Cookbook is an open educational resource for analysing ocean and sea-ice model output in Jupyter notebooks. It has been developed by the Consortium for Ocean--Sea Ice Modelling in Australia (COSIMA) as a community resource for researchers, students, and practitioners working with large gridded datasets, especially output from the ACCESS ocean--sea ice model configurations. The Cookbook is organised around a gastronomy theme: ``Cooking Tutorials'' teach generic, transferable techniques for handling model output, while "Easy Recipes", "Advanced Recipes" and "Regional Specialties" are self-contained notebooks that show how to perform concrete diagnostics and analyses. Along the way, the notebooks demonstrate open-source tools for the scientific analysis of large data, including Intake catalogues, Xarray, Dask, xgcm, xESMF, eofs, Parcels, matplotlib and Cartopy. The Cookbook addresses the steep entry cost of analysing climate model output: it packages expert, often tacit, knowledge into complete, well-documented and reusable workflows, in the same medium in which researchers actually work. It is developed openly on GitHub, is published as a documentation website, and is continuously reviewed and extended by its community through pull requests and regular hackathons. The easy access to data and analysis it provides has contributed to the international adoption of ACCESS ocean and sea-ice model configurations, and has facilitated well over 100 peer-reviewed papers and more than 20 PhD projects.

item.title: A Fitch-Based Wind Farm Parameterization for CM1: Implementation, Validation, and Impacts on Convection Initiation
item.description: arXiv:2611.30806v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We implement a Fitch-based wind farm parameterization in Cloud Model 1 (CM1), representing turbines as elevated momentum sinks and turbulent kinetic energy (TKE) sources within the rotor-swept layer, with optimizations for computational efficiency and parallel execution. Direct comparison with the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model shows close agreement in the magnitude and spatial structure of wind-speed deficits and TKE enhancement. Diurnal simulations also capture the known dependence of boundary layer responses on atmospheric stability, further supporting the consistency of the implementation. Under stable conditions, the wind farm produces coherent spatial patterns in near-surface wind speed and temperature that extend well beyond the farm. In idealized simulations under conditions favorable for convection, large turbines promote convection initiation tens of kilometers downstream, earlier than in the no-farm simulation. Analysis identifies turbulent entrainment of warmer air across the boundary layer top as the dominant source of an elongated downstream warm band, with a smaller contribution from enhanced surface sensible heat flux. Secondary circulations develop across this warm band and provide sustained low-level lifting. A gravity wave generated by the wind farm supplies the initial vertical perturbation, which intensifies as it is advected downstream within an ascending branch of these circulations and develops into a localized deep convective updraft.
item.dc:creator: Jianxiang Li, Zhiyong Meng

item.title: An exact and differentiable rewrite of a coupled weather and fire model
item.description: arXiv:2611.30866v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI is changing weather and climate prediction by replacing physical models with learned ones. Here we show a different path, in which AI coding agents rebuild the physical model itself in a machine-learning framework and reproduce its forecast bit for bit. We reconstruct selected configurations of the Weather Research and Forecasting model and its coupled fire physics in PyTorch, treating every difference from the corrected Fortran code as a bug. Across twelve hours of a Marshall Fire simulation, the two independently advancing codes agree bit for bit at all 365 checkpoints, in the atmosphere, fire and firebrand particles. This agreement holds when the code runs one operation at a time, with the Fortran code's mathematical library. On a separate fast route, the reconstructed model runs about five times faster on one GPU than the double-precision Fortran code on a 128-core CPU node. One backward pass maps the fire's sensitivity to the wind at every grid point. In synthetic tests, its derivatives show how to change wind and fuel moisture to correct a misplaced fire front. Neural networks replace the radiation and fire-spread calculations in 24-hour coupled forecasts, and we measure their effect against the physical calculation. An established model thus becomes fast, differentiable and open to learned components, with its tested calculation intact.
item.dc:creator: John S. Schreck, John Dennis, Iris Linck, Maria Frediani, Pedro A. Jimenez Munoz, Matthew Rehme, Nihanth Cherukuru, David John Gagne II

item.title: A Comparison of Uncertainty in AI and Dynamical Climate Ensembles
item.description: arXiv:2611.31064v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Climate model ensembles and their uncertainty estimates are essential for evaluating risk and designing climate policy. Yet, in the assessment of newly developed AI climate models, evaluating uncertainty is often secondary to diagnosing mean-state climate biases and trends. In this work, we conduct the first systematic comparison of uncertainty representation in ensembles of state-of-the-art AI and dynamical atmospheric climate models. Examining 2-meter temperature, 500 hPa geopotential height, and precipitable water, we find that the AI ensemble exhibits reduced internal variability and model uncertainty across variables relative to the dynamical ensemble. We show that this dampened variability causes the AI ensemble to produce more limited climate extremes and yields underdispersion relative to ERA5. Under a uniform warming scenario, the AI ensemble shows increased model uncertainty. Dynamical models grapple with their own challenges, exhibiting stronger miscalibration (overdispersion) relative to ERA5 and larger climate biases than the AI models. As AI and dynamical climate models are mutually integrated into operational climate prediction, careful consideration of their differences in uncertainty representations is crucial for grounded assessment of climate risk.
item.dc:creator: Jacob B. Landsberg, Devin M. McAfee, M. A. Fernandez, Elizabeth A. Barnes

item.title: ESM-Bench: A Benchmark for Evaluating Whether AI Agents Understand Earth System Model Physics and Code
item.description: arXiv:2611.28477v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AI coding agents that modify Earth System Model (ESM) code must preserve both software interfaces and the physical assumptions encoded in them. We introduce ESM-Bench, a benchmark of 60 developer-commit tasks from 6 repositories: Noah-MP, CLM5, SUMMA, ParFlow, MOM6, and VIC. The v5 corpus contains 17 physics-based bug fixes, 16 process-representation modifications, 13 parameterization-scheme selections, and 14 parameter-optimization tasks. Each task includes a scientific objective, parent-commit source files, a reference diff, and three stored prompt variants. An artifact audit confirms that all 60 reference diffs apply to their supplied starting files. We define an eight-item patch-review rubric and audit five archived patch fixtures against the implemented local checkers. None of the five fixture diffs applies to its supplied starting files, yet three text-pattern checkers return a pass. A ParFlow expression replay disagrees with the reference slopes, and a MOM6 pattern check detects an omitted update. Inspection also identifies a retained VIC reference assignment that overwrites the intended vegetation-specific albedo. These findings expose limits of reference patches and local proxies as correctness evidence. The release provides a reproducible corpus and diagnostic tools; complete expert validation, comparative agent performance, and full-model execution remain unmeasured on v5.
item.dc:creator: Koutian Wu, Yuxuan Cao, Gengchen Mai, Zeping Liu

item.title: Geospatial foundation models and deep learning for climate resilience: a review of transfer, uncertainty and decision readiness
item.description: arXiv:2611.30198v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Geospatial foundation models can reuse information learned from large Earth-observation archives, but their value for climate resilience depends on whether that information transfers to unfamiliar events, regions and observing conditions. This review connects advances in deep learning with the evidence needed for hazard monitoring and early warning. A descriptive audit of 137 full-text hazard-application studies is interpreted alongside a separate corpus of 37 model and benchmark records. Ninety-eight application studies reported an out-of-distribution experiment, whereas headline evaluations included held-out events in 31 studies, regions in 25 and sensors in only two. None of the ten studies coded for geospatial foundation-model fine-tuning used sensor holdout as a headline test. Uncertainty-related methods were recorded in 16 studies, including two with explicitly calibrated probabilistic output. These overlapping counts describe evaluation practice within the coded corpus, not a ranking of model families. We distinguish Earth-observation representation learning from atmospheric forecasting and examine how labels, observability, forecast lead time and decision requirements constrain their contribution across flood, wildfire, drought, heat, cryosphere and cascading-hazard applications. We then develop a decision-backward evaluation framework: define the action and information available when it must be taken, reproduce the relevant shift, retain a matched task-specific baseline, and report misses, false alarms, reliability and end-to-end latency. The framework turns transferability from a broad model claim into a testable requirement for climate adaptation and risk management.
item.dc:creator: Parastoo Farajpoor, Mohammadreza Narimani

item.title: MUNDO: a multiresolution generative framework for temporal downscaling
item.description: arXiv:2611.30868v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Dynamical systems are often observed at coarse temporal resolution through sparse states or temporal aggregates, leaving the underlying fine-scale trajectories unresolved. Recovering these trajectories requires probabilistic models that capture the unresolved variability while remaining consistent with the observations. We present MUNDO (Multiresolution UNified DOwnscaling), a generative framework for temporal downscaling under general linear observation operators. MUNDO introduces a null-space parameterization that enforces exact observation consistency in a single network evaluation, unifying temporal interpolation and disaggregation. To capture complex multiscale dynamics, we leverage reverse Markov learning to factorize the observation operator into a hierarchy of successive coarsenings. Each level models only the degrees of freedom lost between adjacent resolutions. We evaluate MUNDO on two-scale Lorenz-96, four two-dimensional physical systems, and multivariate ERA5 reanalysis over Europe, for both temporal interpolation and disaggregation. Across datasets and tasks, MUNDO generally outperforms flow-based baselines. Single-step MUNDO achieves strong predictive skill, while recursive MUNDO generally improves temporal realism and ensemble calibration, with better spread-skill agreement and predictive coverage.
item.dc:creator: Aymeric Delefosse, Manon Tavernier, Julie Keisler, Anastase Charantonis, Dominique B\'er\'eziat

item.title: A multi-physics Eulerian framework for long-term contrail evolution (MultiCon): Single plume analysis
item.description: arXiv:2509.00965v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present MultiCon, a reduced order, multi-physics Eulerian framework for simulating long term evolution of individual aircraft contrail plumes while retaining essential microphysical processes at low computational cost. The model resolves vertical plume evolution through a coupled PDE system, while horizontal spread is tracked using the method of characteristics and a quasi Gaussian kernel. The current implementation adopts a locally monodisperse approximation. The framework couples the transport of ice particle number and mass, as well as water-vapor transport, with an equation for particle-shape evolution. It also accounts for a- ice-crystal habit evolution and b- turbulence-modulated bulk settling. Habit-dependent growth and sublimation are represented through an approximate inherent growth factor parameterization and a diffusion-limited formulation including latent heat effects. Furthermore, the model incorporates a reduced-order closure for the effective bulk settling velocity, using a Burgers-type model to describe the transition from turbulence-reduced settling towards the terminal velocity of individual particles. We compare MultiCon with CoCiP and APCEMM for a common reference case and a parametric sweep. Across the parameter sweep, MultiCon and APCEMM exhibit similar distributions for most plume diagnostics. In terms of computational cost, CoCiP and MultiCon both operate in the range of tenths of a second to a few seconds per plume simulation. By comparison, for comparable temporal and vertical resolutions, APCEMM requires runtimes on the order of minutes, potentially approaching an hour or more depending on the particle-size bin resolution. Finally, owing to MultiCon's spatially resolved quasi 2D cross-sectional dynamics, selected microphysical processes, and computational efficiency, the solver provides a basis for future global-scale contrail assessments.
item.dc:creator: Amin Jafarimoghaddam, Manuel Soler

item.title: Quantifying AI data center nitrogen oxide (NO$_x$) emissions from space
item.description: arXiv:2608.22153v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: AI data center power demand is spurring rapid deployment of on- and near-site natural gas turbines. The resulting nitrogen oxide NO$_x$ pollution is a growing concern but has not previously been quantified with atmospheric observations. Here we demonstrate space-based detection and quantification of NO$_x$ emissions from the SpaceXAI Colossus 2 power plant in Southaven, Mississippi. Using observations from the geostationary TEMPO satellite instrument, we detect a strong increase in local mean NO$_2$ column concentrations after the plant began operations in late 2025. We then use TEMPO to estimate two-week-average NO$_x$ source rates from August 2025 to August 2026, calibrating against continuous emission monitoring system (CEMS) data from US power plants. TEMPO first detected NO$_x$ emissions in December 2025 at 530$\pm$220 kg h$^{-1}$. We find that emissions increased through August 2026, averaging 870$\pm$165 kg h$^{-1}$ after February 2026, roughly 19$\pm$4 times higher than expected from the facility's March 2026 permit for 41 turbines operating under best available control technology (BACT) requirements ($\sim$47 kg h$^{-1}$). Emissions at the expected level would be undetectable by our TEMPO analysis.
item.dc:creator: Kevin D. Gauld, Daniel J. Varon, Nicholas Balasus, Daniel H. Cusworth

item.title: A Station-Based Evaluation of Machine Learning-based Weather Forecasting Models in Northern Norway
item.description: arXiv:2609.10564v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent machine learning weather prediction (MLWP) models have demonstrated remarkable forecasting skill on global reanalysis-based benchmarks. However, their performance remains unclear in challenging environments such as Northern Norway, where narrow fjords and rapidly changing weather result in highly variable local wind conditions. In this case study, we evaluate FourCastNet3 (FCN3), GraphCast, and ECMWF High Resolution Forecast (HRES) for wind speed forecasting using multi-year station observations from Northern Norway, focusing on their relative performance, generalization beyond the training period, and performance under high-wind conditions. Our results show that HRES slightly outperforms FCN3 and GraphCast, with an overall RMSE of 2.89 $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, compared to 2.96 $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ for FCN3 and 2.94 $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ for GraphCast. Notably, the MLWP models maintain comparable performance beyond their respective training periods, with no clear evidence of noticeable degradation. FCN3 performs best under high-wind conditions, although all models substantially underestimate strong winds. Our findings suggest that MLWP has become competitive with NWP for local wind, but further refinements are still needed to capture complex terrain better.
item.dc:creator: Siyan Chen, Lars Uebbing, Eirik Mikal Samuelsen, Georgios Leontidis, Arnt-B{\o}rre Salberg, S\'ebastien Lef\`evre, Robert Jenssen, Kristoffer Wickstr{\o}m

item.title: Condensation-related expansion work of water vapor as a major pathway for kinetic energy generation in the lower atmosphere
item.description: arXiv:2611.20813v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Earth's atmosphere operates a steam cycle: water evaporates from the surface, expands as vapor, condenses in colder air, and returns as precipitation. Yet its power and relationship to atmospheric mechanical power remain poorly quantified. Applying the Clausius--Clapeyron relation between saturated vapor expansion work and latent heat converted at Carnot efficiency to vertically distributed condensation, we derive the steam-engine power as a sum of the gravitational and condensation-related contributions, $W_v=W_g+W_c$; it is not the net power of a complete moist-air cycle. Using twelve years of GPM/DPR spectral latent-heating profiles and MERRA-2 fields, we estimate $W_v\simeq4.1$ W m$^{-2}$, with $W_c\simeq2.8$ W m$^{-2}$. Separately, we diagnose total atmospheric mechanical power $W=W_P+W_K\simeq4.3$ W m$^{-2}$, comprising gravitational power of precipitation $W_P\simeq1.1$ W m$^{-2}$ and kinetic energy generation $W_K\simeq3.2$ W m$^{-2}$, including $2.4$ W m$^{-2}$ below 500 hPa. Both correspondences $W_v\simeq W$ and $W_c\simeq W_K$ lie within 20--30% uncertainty estimates. To explain these correspondences, we propose that $W_c$ generates the potential energy associated with surface pressure gradients. Cross-isobaric flow in the frictional lower atmosphere converts this energy into kinetic energy. In a horizontally isothermal atmosphere, this positive pressure work would be nearly cancelled by compression aloft. An idealized circulation illustrates how differential heating can offset compression, allowing nearly isobaric upper return flow. In the proposed mechanism, condensation-driven circulation unlocks this thermal compensation thus providing a major pathway for lower-atmospheric kinetic energy generation. We discuss how changes in the coupling between condensation and differential heating could test this proposed causal relationship.
item.dc:creator: Anastassia M. Makarieva, Andrei V. Nefiodov

item.title: Natural analogs for geoengineering suggest modest radiative plant gains
item.description: arXiv:2611.26845v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Stratospheric aerosol injection (SAI) to limit global warming overshoot would reduce total solar radiation while increasing the proportion of diffuse light reaching Earth's surface, creating competing effects on plant growth. Analog studies using volcanic eruptions show impacts ranging from significantly negative to strongly positive, and numerical models suggest radiative effects from SAI would range from neutral to slightly positive. Here we show, using eddy covariance measurements at eight AmeriFlux sites (four maize and four forest), that radiative effects of smoke are positive across sites. This suggests that radiative effects from SAI would likely be modest but positive, consistent with numerical models. We attribute inconsistencies in the literature to limitations in the underlying assumptions and methods of previous analog studies; addressing these issues brings their results into agreement with our findings. More broadly, our results suggest that aerosols from wildfires, volcanoes, pollution, and SAI tend to moderately enhance photosynthesis.
item.dc:creator: Brendan Clark, Ben Kravitz, Daniele Visioni, Manuel Lerdau

item.title: A high-order IMEX-DG solver for atmospheric dynamics: rotating tests on non-conforming meshes
item.description: arXiv:2605.29598v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We present a high-order implicit-explicit discontinuous Galerkin (IMEX-DG) solver for the compressible Euler equations that accounts for rotational effects within an atmospheric framework. Time integration follows a second-order additive Runge-Kutta scheme, treating stiff acoustic modes implicitly and advective terms explicitly. The solver is built on the deal.II finite element library, combining matrix-free operator evaluation, adaptive non-conforming mesh capabilities, and distributed-memory parallelism. The inclusion of rotation extends the framework to large-scale atmospheric dynamics, where the Coriolis force plays a central role in geostrophic balance. Its incorporation into a high-order matrix-free DG discretisation is, however, non-trivial, as it requires a careful formulation of the discrete rotational operator. Two alternative treatments of the rotational and gravitational source terms within the solution strategy, based on nonlinear fixed-point iterations, are therefore introduced and compared in terms of accuracy, robustness, and computational efficiency. A discrete analysis of the rotational operator is also carried out in order to derive a formulation suitable for efficient matrix-free implementation. The proposed formulation is verified through convergence studies on rotating inertia-gravity wave benchmarks and further assessed in fully three-dimensional simulations of stratified flow over orography on both uniform and adaptive meshes. The numerical results show that the rotating IMEX-DG framework has the expected accuracy and stability properties while correctly capturing the asymmetry and wave structures induced by rotation in large-scale atmospheric flows.
item.dc:creator: Letizia Bottani, Tommaso Benacchio, Giuseppe Orlando, Luca Bonaventura, Allan Peter Engsig-Karup

item.title: How Wet-Biased Datasets Shape the Training and Mislead the Evaluation of Generative Precipitation Nowcasting
item.description: arXiv:2610.26486v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Generative models for precipitation nowcasting are trained and evaluated predominantly on wet-biased datasets, which over-represent precipitation events to emphasize rare extremes. Selecting test cases based on target observations is known to favor forecasts that match the selected distribution rather than the intended deployment distribution. We show analytically that the same target-dependent selection, applied to the training set, tilts the conditional distribution learned by an ideal generative model by exactly the factor that such an evaluation rewards. We test both evaluation and training effects with a satellite-to-radar diffusion model in a controlled experiment that crosses wet-biased and uniform sampling of the training and of the test set. The evaluation effect appears in full: the same model looks under-predictive on a wet-biased test set but over-predicts light rain on a deployment-consistent one, whichever way it was trained. Inverse probability weighting recovers the deployment scores from the wet-biased set. The training effect is real but partial: the model trained on wet-biased data forecasts more rain than its uniformly trained counterpart, yet remains far from calibrated even on a test set drawn like its training set, and gains skill for rain at a modest cost in calibration. Wet-biased training is thus a trade-off, not an error. Using classifier-free guidance as an example of a tuned quantity, we show how this misdirects model development: most scores on the wet-biased test set favor the largest guidance scale, whereas calibration, frequency bias, and a threshold-weighted proper score on the deployment-consistent set favor the smallest.
item.dc:creator: Christoph Metzl, Stefan Kapsreiter, Kianusch Vahid Yousefnia, Virginia Poli, Richard M\"uller, Frank Kr\"uger, Tobias B\"olle
